paras: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb took place on the night of Thursday, October 11, 1888, when armed and masked men boarded and searched a passenger train at Francisco, Gibson County, Indiana, looking for Grubb, who was charged with the murder of Gertrude Downey. Grubb was not aboard, having been taken to Vincennes by another route, and the men left the train without harming anyone. A Princeton wire report carried the story to papers in Pennsylvania, Texas and Delaware as a lynching "narrowly averted".

Grubb, a 24-year-old Gibson County man, had courted Downey, whose family lived at Francisco, eight miles east of Princeton, and she had refused to marry him. On September 13 he met her at the Princeton fair grounds and shot her with a revolver; she died of her wounds on September 19.

Threats of mob violence followed at once, and the sheriff, fearing an attack on the jail, moved Grubb to Evansville. A crowd reportedly "started into town on two different nights" from Downey's neighborhood but turned back, and Evansville jail officers were warned of a Gibson County movement to lynch him. He was later held at Jeffersonville; an October 13 notice placed him in the State Prison South until his trial.

On Thursday, October 11, Grubb was brought from Jeffersonville to Vincennes for trial, and the move, according to the Indianapolis Journal's Vincennes correspondent, "developed a mob of masked men". Two of them boarded the Air-line train at Oakland City to look for Grubb and were to signal at Francisco if he was aboard. Francisco was a flag station, and the Journal said the train stopped there because the leader of the Princeton band, a passenger "innocent of the mob's plan", flagged it to ride home.

Eight men then entered each coach, inspected every face, and left the train without a word when Grubb was not found. The Princeton wire said only that the men expected the sheriff to bring Grubb through Francisco on the evening train, searched it, and missed him because the sheriff had taken another train.

Grubb's trial for murder opened in the Knox Circuit Court at Vincennes on October 12, with a plea of insanity as his defense. The jury found him guilty of first-degree murder and, after eight hours, fixed the penalty at death; sentence was read on October 19. A Vincennes dispatch of October 27 reported that he had been sentenced to be hanged on April 19. No report of arrests or of any inquiry into the men who searched the train appears in the coverage.

Two separate accounts circulated: a short Princeton wire and a longer special to the Indianapolis Journal from Vincennes, which the Rock Island Daily Argus condensed under the headline "The Lynchers Got Left". The wire ran as "Lynchers Outwitted" in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and as "A Disappointed Mob" in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, and the Wilmington Daily Republican summarized it among the day's news. The wire called Grubb "the slayer of Miss Gertrude Downey" and "the murderer" before his trial, and the Lancaster version said that "Fortunately" the sheriff had taken another train and the mob "was cheated of its victim."

The Journal's headline, "A Mob of Would-Be Lynchers Boards the Wrong Train in Quest of a Murderer," treated the search as a near miss and passed no judgment on the masked men. Indiana papers were hostile to Grubb throughout: the Journal called him "the fiend" in September and praised the jury's "moral courage" in imposing death. None of the reports gave the race of Grubb, Downey or the men on the train.

Most reports put the band at sixty, but the Lancaster printing of the Princeton wire said "a hundred men". The Lancaster printing's October 13 dateline and "last night" would place the search on October 12, but the Fort Worth printing of the same text was dated October 12 and the Wilmington summary said Thursday night. The Journal said the mob expected Grubb on the Ohio & Mississippi road, though its scouts rode the Air-line; the Argus said the mob expected the Air-Line and he came over the Ohio & Mississippi.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb
bases: Armed, masked men stopped and searched a train at Francisco to seize Sylvester Grubb, an accused murderer in the sheriff's charge, and the papers called them would-be lynchers; they did not find him (A2, A3, A5).

A group of sixty (or a hundred) armed, masked men searched a train to lynch Grubb for the killing of Gertrude Downey, but he was not aboard and no one was killed or hurt (A2, A3, A5, A6). It was an attempted lynching; Grubb was later tried and sentenced to death (A8, A10).

Two independently datelined reports, a Princeton wire (A2, A5, A6) and the Indianapolis Journal's Vincennes special (A3, condensed in A4), agree that masked men searched the train at Francisco for Grubb and left without finding him.

accounts.label: Princeton wire
accounts.gist: The sheriff was expected to pass through Francisco with Grubb on the evening train; sixty (or a hundred) armed, masked men boarded and searched it, but the sheriff had taken another train.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal Vincennes special
accounts.gist: Grubb was brought from Jeffersonville to Vincennes by another road; two scouts rode the Air-line train from Oakland City to signal at Francisco, where a passenger happened to flag the train, and eight men per coach inspected faces and left without a word.

framing.detail: The Princeton wire ran as 'Lynchers Outwitted' and 'A Disappointed Mob', saying 'Fortunately' the sheriff had taken another train and the mob was 'cheated of its victim'.
The Indianapolis Journal headlined 'A Mob of Would-Be Lynchers Boards the Wrong Train in Quest of a Murderer' and described the search without comment on the men.
Indiana coverage called Grubb 'the fiend' and praised the jury's 'moral courage' in imposing death, while reporting the moves made to keep him from mobs.

conflicts.note: The Lancaster reprint of the Princeton wire says a hundred; the Fort Worth printing of the same wire and the Journal's separate account both say sixty.
A2's text matches A5's Oct. 12 dispatch nearly word for word, so its Oct. 13 dateline is likely a re-dating; A6 and A3 point to Thursday, Oct. 11.
